(2) This National Policy Statement applies to all activities managed under the Resource Management Act 1991, except for infrastructure (as defined in the Act) and primary production (as defined in the National Planning Standards).
(3) This National Policy Statement applies to all environments and all zones, including coastal environments. Where there is a conflict between the provisions of this National Policy Statement and the New Zealand Coastal Policy Statement 2010, the New Zealand Coastal Policy Statement 2010 prevails.
(4) This National Policy Statement does not preclude decision-makers from managing natural hazard risk beyond its application, including risks from other natural hazards and from activities not otherwise covered, or from applying a more conservative approach to the natural hazard risks that it does cover.
(5) This National Policy Statement does not override any existing use rights that may apply under section 10 of the Act.

text:
Proportionate management of natural hazard risk
(1) Decision-makers must consider the scale and detail of information necessary to assess the risk, having regard to the anticipated level of risk.
(2) When managing natural hazard risk associated with subdivision, use and development, decision-makers must apply mitigation measures, including location and design, for the purposes of ensuring that: (a) very high natural hazard risk is avoided; (b) high or medium natural hazard risk is avoided or mitigated proportionate to the level of risk; and (c) any creation of, or increase in, significant natural hazard risk on other sites is avoided or mitigated proportionate to the level of natural hazard risk.
(3) When applying the proportionate approach required by (2)(b) and (2)(c), decision-makers must take into account the cost effectiveness of mitigation measures relative to the level of anticipated risk.

text:
What the NPS-NH is trying to achieve
The aim of the NPS-NH is to maximise development while minimising losses from natural hazard events — in terms of injury, loss of life, and damage to land and buildings — by encouraging the right kind of development in the right locations.
To achieve this, the NPS-NH directs that a risk-based proportionate approach be applied. This means first considering the likelihood of a natural hazard event and its potential consequences for people and property, rather than just the presence of a hazard, and then applying a management response proportionate to the level of risk posed.
The NPS-NH does not direct exact outcomes, apart from the avoidance of very high risk. Management of natural hazard risk is highly context specific: communities have different risk exposure, different social and economic drivers, and different tolerance of risk.

text:
The NPS-NH is designed to apply to resource consenting
Section 104(1)(b)(iii) of the RMA requires decision-makers to have regard to any relevant national policy statement when deciding a subdivision or land-use consent. This applies until the decision is made, even if the application was lodged before the NPS-NH came into force.
For discretionary and non-complying activities, all relevant matters can be considered under section 104B, so consent authorities must have regard to relevant provisions of the NPS-NH.
Under sections 104A (controlled activities) and 104C (restricted discretionary activities), the consent authority can only consider the NPS-NH if natural hazards are explicitly included in the matters over which discretion or control has been restricted in the plan.
Sections 106 and 106A allow a consent authority to refuse consent, or grant it subject to conditions, if it considers that there is a significant risk from natural hazards. These sections can be used for any consent type.

text:
The NPS-NH applies to specified natural hazards
Flooding refers to inundation of land that is normally dry. It includes fluvial flooding, where waterways overflow their banks; pluvial flooding, where intense rainfall exceeds drainage capacity or soil absorption; and groundwater flooding, where the water table rises above the surface, often after prolonged rainfall.
Landslips refers to the downhill movement of soil, rock or debris under gravity, which may be triggered by rainfall or earthquake shaking. Types include rockfalls, topples, slides, flows and creep.
Coastal erosion refers to the retreat of the shoreline, temporarily or permanently, due to tides and waves including storm surges. Coastal inundation refers to inundation of land by seawater, including by storm surges and high tides.
Active faults refers to faults that have ruptured the surface in the past, as identified in the New Zealand Active Faults Database.
Liquefaction, including lateral spread, refers to loose, water-saturated soils losing strength due to earthquake shaking.
Tsunami refers to a series of long-period waves, primarily generated by underwater earthquake events where there is significant displacement of the seafloor.

text:
Activities excluded — infrastructure and primary production

text:
The NPS-NH does not automatically override existing planning provisions
The NPS-NH sets a national baseline for managing natural hazard risk through land-use planning. Many district plans already include risk-based approaches that use different likelihood thresholds, consequence measures and risk matrices.

Where an existing planning approach would prevent development that the NPS-NH risk matrix would assess as lower than very high risk, decision-makers may choose to apply those planning provisions rather than follow the NPS-NH.
Where a plan includes existing risk-based provisions for natural hazards, a first step should be assessing them against the NPS-NH approach to determine whether they are more permissive, the same, or more conservative.

text:
Determining the likelihood level
Likelihood is the chance of something happening. The likelihood table uses two measures: probability of exceedance — the probability that a hazard event of a certain size will occur or be exceeded in a given time period, referred to as annual exceedance probability (AEP) when that period is one year; and average recurrence interval (ARI), the average period between hazard events of a given magnitude, often called a return period.
The likelihood table includes seven levels based on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change likelihood scale, adjusted for New Zealand natural hazard management terminology. Qualitative descriptors range from almost certain to very rare.
District plans often do not seek to manage events with a likelihood more frequent than 1% AEP, and councils may not hold data on those events. In these circumstances the use of best available information may be relied on.
If a council holds information for a particular natural hazard at a range of likelihoods, it should manage the impacts of the likelihood event that results in the highest level of risk under the matrix.

text:
Determining the consequence level
Consequence generally refers to the impact of a natural hazard event on the built, social, economic or natural environments. The NPS-NH consequence table focuses on consequences for property — buildings and land — and for people, in terms of injuries or fatalities.

text:
Residual risk
Clause 3.2(2)(b) requires decision-makers to consider the residual risk associated with any existing or proposed mitigation measures. Residual risk is the risk that remains after risk treatment measures — avoidance or mitigation — have been applied.
Any new development in hazard-prone areas, even with mitigation measures, will result in an increase in exposure and an increase in overall risk.
At the consenting scale, it is most often hard structural measures, such as catch nets for slope instability, or design measures, such as minimum floor levels for flooding, that are proposed. These are designed to protect against a particular likelihood event, and residual risk arises from the potential occurrence of an event beyond the design threshold of the mitigation measure.
Decision-makers should be aware that extreme events exceeding design thresholds are possible, and may need to prepare emergency management plans and response strategies. Intensifying housing in areas protected by hard structures may increase risk to life in an extreme event that overtops defences.

text:
Impacts of climate change
Policy 6 requires a risk assessment to consider the potential impacts of climate change to at least 100 years into the future. The 100-year timeframe applies when using existing hazard data and information in the risk assessment process.
If information that includes climate change over the 100-year timeframe is not available or applicable, Policy 5 — assessment and decisions must be based on the best available information — applies.
There is no single statutory requirement mandating a specific future projection. The national adaptation plan is principles-based rather than prescriptive, and recommends consideration of a range of plausible future conditions, and tailoring the scenario used to suit the longevity and significance of the activity being considered.
The impacts of climate change will increase the likelihood of climate-sensitive hazards such as flooding and rainfall-induced landslips. What is currently a 1% AEP event may in future become a 2% AEP event, and at the same time have increased consequences, so what is a low risk now may become a high risk in the future.
Changes to the risk profile under different climate scenarios can be assessed using the matrix in two ways: by holding the event likelihood constant and adjusting the consequence rating to reflect increased impacts; or by assessing how an event of a given magnitude may increase in likelihood over time.

text:
Managing risk proportionately
The NPS-NH directs decision-makers to respond proportionately to natural hazard risk. When risk is higher, stronger constraints on development are appropriate; when risk is low, development should be enabled.
The intended outcome is that new development likely to be badly damaged by natural hazards does not progress, and that any limitation on, or required mitigation measure for, new development is justified.
Clause 3.3(2) provides the framework: very high risk is avoided; high or medium risk is avoided or mitigated proportionate to the level of risk; and any creation of, or increase in, significant risk on other sites is avoided or mitigated proportionate to the level of risk.
The NPS-NH is not intended to limit the way decision-makers manage risks below the very high threshold. Policies and rules in existing plans that avoid new development at a risk level below very high continue to apply.

Significant natural hazard risk is defined for the purposes of the NPS-NH as natural hazard risk assessed as medium, high or very high using the risk matrix.

text:
When a detailed risk assessment is required
Under clause 3.3(1), decision-makers must have regard to the anticipated level of risk when considering the scale and detail of information necessary.
Most natural hazard data held by a local authority is at region-wide or district-wide scale and is either susceptibility or hazard information. That type of information indicates where an area is likely to be affected by a natural hazard, and may mean that deciding an application requires a request to the applicant for a further detailed assessment of the risk by a suitably qualified and experienced person (SQEP).
Any risk assessment prepared by an SQEP to support a consent application should align with the NPS-NH framework. Depending on the level of risk, it may also be appropriate for the consent authority to have the applicant's risk assessment peer reviewed by an SQEP before deciding the application.
As a general guide, an SQEP is a person who is independent; has a relevant professional registration, such as chartered professional engineer; applies good professional practice; undertakes a risk assessment in accordance with accepted industry practice and guidelines; and is willing to certify and stand by the conclusions of the report.
Regional or district-scale susceptibility mapping is therefore an indicator of the need for further assessment, not a substitute for a site-specific assessment.

text:
Applying the best available information
Clause 3.4 seeks to ensure decision-making is based on the best information available at the time. This means using complete and scientifically robust data where possible, but it does not preclude using information that is uncertain or incomplete.
The direction to use the best available information allows decision-makers to actively manage risks even when the information is not perfect. The alternative — delaying action because of uncertainty about the exact risk profile — means people and property stay at risk.
Applying best available information involves: using complete and scientifically robust data where possible; recognising that best available information may include modelling output, partial data and information from other sources; giving preference, when information is uncertain or incomplete, to sources providing the greatest level of certainty while taking all practicable steps to reduce uncertainty; and interpreting uncertain information in a way that gives effect to the proportionate risk-based approach.
Local authorities should develop their own criteria for evaluating the suitability of information — for example, the age of the information; advances in science or changes in the environment since publication; the qualifications and experience of the author; whether it was peer reviewed; whether it follows best practice methods; and whether uncertainties and limitations are well documented.

Interaction with other policies and legislation
Natural hazard risk is also addressed through other legislation. The Building Act 2004 addresses building requirements through the Building Code and related compliance pathways. The Civil Defence Emergency Management Act 2002 focuses on preparing for, responding to and recovering from natural hazard events. The Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act 1987 requires all known natural hazard information held by a council to be included on Land Information Memoranda.

text:
Issue — Risks from naturally occurring events
Canterbury is subject to a range of naturally occurring events including flooding, earthquake, liquefaction, lateral spread, land instability, coastal erosion, sea water inundation and tsunami.
When these events occur they can cause adverse effects on the social, economic and cultural wellbeing of people and communities. Infrastructure and property may be damaged, activity can be disrupted, and human health can be put at risk.
Natural hazard events can also have flow-on effects on the natural environment. For example, a flood may result in sewage being inadvertently discharged into a waterway.

Subdivision, use and development of land can increase the risk from natural hazards, by placing more people and property in the path of hazard events and by changing the way hazard events behave.
Development can also transfer risk. Filling, earthworks and flood-protection works on one site can displace floodwater onto neighbouring land.
Decisions about where and how development occurs are therefore a primary means of managing natural hazard risk.

Policy — Avoidance of inappropriate development in high hazard areas
To avoid new subdivision, use and development, except as provided for in Policy 11.3.4, of land in high hazard areas, unless the subdivision, use or development:
1. is not likely to result in loss of life or serious injuries in the event of a natural hazard occurrence; and
2. is not likely to suffer significant damage or loss in the event of a natural hazard occurrence; and
3. is not likely to require new or upgraded hazard mitigation works to mitigate or avoid the natural hazard; and
4. is not likely to exacerbate the effects of the natural hazard; or
5. outside of greater Christchurch, is proposed to be located in an area zoned or identified in a district plan for urban residential, industrial or commercial use at the date of notification of the CRPS, in which case the effects of the natural hazard must be mitigated; or
6. within greater Christchurch, is proposed to be located in an area zoned in a district plan for urban residential, industrial or commercial use, or identified as a Greenfield Priority Area, at the date the Land Use Recovery Plan was notified, in which case the effect of the natural hazard must be avoided or appropriately mitigated; or
7. within greater Christchurch, relates to the maintenance or upgrading of existing critical or significant infrastructure.

text:
Policy — Avoid development in areas subject to inundation
In areas not subject to Policy 11.3.1 that are subject to inundation by a 0.5% AEP flood event, any new subdivision, use and development, excluding critical infrastructure, shall be avoided unless there is no increased risk to life and the subdivision, use or development:
1. is of a type that is not likely to suffer material damage in an inundation event; or
2. is ancillary or incidental to the main development; or
3. meets all of the following criteria: (a) new buildings have an appropriate floor level above the 0.5% AEP design flood level; and (b) hazardous substances will not be inundated during a 0.5% AEP flood event;
provided that a higher standard of management of inundation hazard events may be adopted where local catchment conditions warrant, as determined by a cost/benefit assessment.
When determining areas subject to inundation, climate change projections including sea-level rise are to be taken into account.
A 0.5% AEP flood means there is a 1 in 200 chance that a flood of this size will happen in any given year. A 1% AEP flood means there is a 1 in 100 chance in any given year.
This policy implements Objective 11.2.1.

New subdivision, use and development of land on or close to an active earthquake fault trace, or in areas susceptible to liquefaction and lateral spreading, shall be managed in order to avoid or mitigate the adverse effects of fault rupture, liquefaction and lateral spreading.

text:
Policy — General risk management approach
For natural hazards or areas not addressed by Policies 11.3.1, 11.3.2 and 11.3.3, subdivision, use or development of land shall be avoided if the risk from natural hazards is unacceptable.
When determining whether risk is unacceptable, the following matters will be considered: 1. the likelihood of the natural hazard event; and 2. the potential consequence of the natural hazard event for people and communities, property and infrastructure, the environment, and emergency response organisations.
Where there is uncertainty in the likelihood or consequences of a natural hazard event, the local authority shall adopt a precautionary approach.
Formal risk management techniques should be used, such as AS/NZS ISO 31000 Risk Management or AS/NZS 1170.0 Structural Design Actions.
This policy implements Objective 11.2.1.

text:
Definition — High hazard areas
For the purposes of Chapter 11, high hazard areas are:
1. flood hazard areas subject to inundation events where the water depth in metres multiplied by the velocity in metres per second is greater than or equal to 1, or where depths are greater than 1 metre, in a 0.2% AEP flood event;
2. land outside of greater Christchurch subject to coastal erosion over the next 100 years;
3. land within greater Christchurch likely to be subject to coastal erosion, including the cumulative effects of sea-level rise, over the next 100 years; and
4. land subject to sea water inundation, excluding tsunami, over the next 100 years.
The flood component of this definition is a test applied to a 0.2% AEP event, that is, a 1 in 500 year event. Flood modelling supplied for a different design event, such as a 1% or 0.5% AEP event, does not by itself establish whether a site is inside or outside a high hazard area. Where only a different design event is available, that limitation should be stated rather than treated as a result.
International research and observation have shown that critical flood depths and velocities damage structures and harm people. In water that is not moving, flood depths greater than about 1 metre pose a threat to life. Where water is moving, velocity increases the risk to life and property, and depth and velocity combined can result in significant risk.

text:
Overview — scope of the chapter
A natural hazard is defined in the Resource Management Act 1991 as any atmospheric, earth or water related occurrence — including earthquake, tsunami, erosion, volcanic and geothermal activity, landslip, subsidence, sedimentation, wind, drought, fire or flooding — the action of which adversely affects or may adversely affect human life, property, or other aspects of the environment.
Both the Canterbury Regional Policy Statement 2013 and the New Zealand Coastal Policy Statement 2010 promote a risk-based approach to natural hazard and coastal hazard management.
The Council has defined a risk-based approach as: managing risk when there is uncertain or insufficient natural hazard risk information; and managing risk based on the scale of a particular natural hazard event, together with the likelihood of that event occurring and the effects on people and property.
This approach reflects the large geographical spread of the District, with sparse population and low development in some areas compared with discrete areas of larger population in its townships. In the larger populated and developed areas the consequences from natural hazards, and therefore the risk, could be considerably greater.
The natural hazards managed by this Plan are coastal hazards, flood hazards, geotechnical hazards, and wildfire hazards.

text:
Overlays used in this chapter
The chapter manages natural hazards through mapped overlays. Those relevant to this extract are the Plains Flood Management Overlay and the Waimakariri Flood Management Overlay. The chapter also uses the Coastal Erosion Overlay, Coastal Inundation Overlay, Tsunami Policy Overlay, Greendale Fault Overlay, Fault Investigation Overlay and Fault Awareness Overlay, which are outside the scope of this assessment.
An overlay applies in addition to the underlying zone provisions. A site may therefore be subject both to the overlay provisions and to the rules of its zone.
The two flood overlays carry different rules. Within the Plains Flood Management Overlay a new residential unit or principal building is permitted subject to the NH-R2.3 conditions. Within the Waimakariri Flood Management Overlay the same activity is non-complying under NH-R2.5.
Teaching note. The presence of an overlay indicates mapped hazard exposure. The absence of an overlay on a supplied record is not evidence that a site is free from that hazard; it may mean only that the site has not been mapped, or that the supplied record does not include overlay information. The chapter itself recognises this in the Overview, which describes the Council's risk-based approach as including managing risk when there is uncertain or insufficient natural hazard risk information.

High hazard area, important infrastructure, land transport infrastructure, principal building and residential unit are terms defined in the Definitions chapter of the Partially Operative Selwyn District Plan. Those definitions are not part of the Natural Hazards chapter and are not reproduced in this extract.
Teaching note. Because the district definition of high hazard area is not in the supplied corpus, the applicable definition available to your system is the regional one, in Canterbury Regional Policy Statement Chapter 11 (document CRPS_CH11, clause 'Definition: high hazard areas'). That definition applies a test at a 0.2% AEP event: water depth in metres multiplied by velocity in metres per second greater than or equal to 1, or depth greater than 1 metre.
Teaching note. A response that classifies a site as inside or outside a high hazard area should say which definition it applied and at which design event, and should state that flood evidence supplied for a more frequent event, such as a 1% or 0.5% AEP event, cannot be substituted into a test defined for the 0.2% AEP event.

Policy — High hazard areas
Avoid new subdivision, use, or development of land in high hazard areas, except for important infrastructure and land transport infrastructure where NH-P2 applies instead, unless the subdivision, use or development either:
1. is not likely to: (a) result in loss of life or serious injuries; and (b) suffer significant damage or loss; and (c) require new or upgraded natural hazard mitigation works to mitigate or avoid the natural hazard; and (d) exacerbate the effects of the natural hazard; or
2. alternatively, is located in any of the following areas as at 6 December 2013, in which case the effects of the natural hazard must be avoided or appropriately mitigated: (a) a Living 1 zone, Living X zone or Living Z zone; (b) in Lincoln, a Living 2 zone; or (c) a Business zone.
Teaching note. Limb 1 requires all four of (a) to (d) to be satisfied. A proposal that would place people in the area, or that relies on new mitigation works, does not satisfy limb 1.

Policy — Important infrastructure in high hazard areas
Avoid the development or use of land, buildings, or structures in high hazard areas for any important infrastructure or land transport infrastructure, unless the activity:
1. does not pose a significant risk, or exacerbate an existing risk, to people or property; and

3. contributes to the resilience of the community in the event of a natural disaster.

text:
Policy — Plains Flood Management Overlay
In areas within the Plains Flood Management Overlay that are not a high hazard area, provide for:
1. important infrastructure and land transport infrastructure; and
2. any other new subdivision, use, and development only where every new residential unit or principal building has an appropriate floor level above the 200 year Average Return Interval (ARI) design flood level.
Teaching note. This policy states the requirement qualitatively as an appropriate floor level. The numeric standard is set by NH-SCHED1, which specifies a minimum finished floor level 300 mm above the 200-year ARI flood level. Assess a proposed floor level against NH-SCHED1 and the rule NH-R2.3, not against this policy alone.
Teaching note. Where no Flood Assessment Certificate has been issued for the site, the design flood level has not been established and a proposed floor level cannot be evaluated against this policy on the supplied information.

Policy — Defences against water
Avoid locating any residential unit or other asset of high value, including important infrastructure, between any waterbody and any defence against water designed or used to contain floodwater from that waterbody, unless that asset has a functional need or operational need to be in that location.

text:
Policy — Earthworks in flood management overlays
Manage earthworks undertaken in the Waimakariri Flood Management Overlay and the Plains Flood Management Overlay to ensure that they do not exacerbate flooding on any other property by displacing or diverting floodwater on surrounding land.
Teaching note. Earthworks that raise ground level within a flood management overlay reduce flood storage and can raise flood levels on adjoining land. The volume displaced and its effect on surrounding flood levels are the matters this policy is directed at. An assertion that a proposal will not increase flood risk on other sites is not sufficient without supporting analysis of the changed flood levels and flow paths.

text:
Policy — Liquefaction
Provide for subdivision on flat land where the liquefaction hazard has been appropriately identified and assessed, and can be adequately remedied or mitigated.
Teaching note. Regional or district-scale susceptibility mapping indicates the possible presence of liquefiable ground. It does not establish the liquefaction hazard on an individual site, and it is not a substitute for a site-specific geotechnical assessment by a suitably qualified and experienced person.
Teaching note. Where a site-specific geotechnical assessment has not been provided, the liquefaction hazard has not been appropriately identified and assessed for the purposes of this policy.

text:
Rule — New buildings and structures in the Plains Flood Management Overlay
Within the Plains Flood Management Overlay, the establishment of any new residential unit or other principal building is a permitted activity (PER) where:
a. the building is not located in a high hazard area; and
b. the building is not located between any surface water body and any stopbank designed to contain floodwater from that surface water body; and
c. the building finished floor level is equal to or higher than the minimum floor level stated in a Flood Assessment Certificate issued in accordance with NH-SCHED1 Flood Assessment Certificates.
Teaching note. Compliance is assessed against the certified minimum finished floor level. A proposed floor level described only as raised, or as having some freeboard, without reference to a certified design flood level, does not demonstrate compliance with (c).

text:
Rule — Activity status where NH-R2.3 is not met
Where compliance with NH-R2.3.a or NH-R2.3.b is not achieved, the activity is non-complying (NC).
Where compliance with NH-R2.3.c is not achieved, the activity is restricted discretionary (RDIS).
Teaching note. The two failure paths are not equivalent. Being in a high hazard area, or between a water body and its stopbank, makes the activity non-complying, which is a substantially higher consent hurdle. Failing only the certified floor level makes it restricted discretionary. A response that treats any non-compliance with NH-R2.3 as merely requiring consent understates the first case.

text:
Schedule — Flood Assessment Certificates
A Flood Assessment Certificate will be issued by the Selwyn District Council, valid for 2 years from the date of issue, which specifies:
1. whether or not the site or activity is located on land that is within a High Hazard Area; and
2. whether or not the site or activity is likely to be subject to inundation in a 200-year Average Recurrence Interval (ARI) flood event; and
3. where the site or activity is not located on land within a High Hazard Area but is likely to be subject to inundation in a 200-year ARI flood event, a minimum finished floor level for any new building or structure, or part of one, that is 300 mm above the 200-year ARI flood level.
The minimum finished floor level will be determined with reference to: 1. the most up to date models and maps held by Selwyn District Council or Canterbury Regional Council; 2. any relevant field information; and 3. any site-specific flood assessment prepared by a suitably qualified and experienced person.
Advice note. Information showing the modelled flood characteristics within specific parts of the district is publicly available online via Canterbury Maps. That information is indicative only and will be updated to reflect the best information as it becomes available.
